coverage.note: Objectives, the volume baseline, FR/NFR IDs, principles, confirmed decisions, backlog and the readiness table are explicit and traceable. Main clarity defects: the unit and scope of the FR-8 tolerance, and a confirmed decision that depends on an unrecorded pending item.

Checked idempotency, CDE scoping, DR, the latency budget, reconciliation timing, the build phase order against FR-9, SAD handling, HSM availability, DynamoDB capacity and payout-account control. Several requirements (FR-5, NFR-2, NFR-4, NFR-5, NFR-8, FR-9) cannot be met as written. The ledger, money handling and webhooks are fit for purpose.

Findings that challenge approved decisions: Aurora Global DR against zero RPO (FND-003), and one HSM at launch against NFR-3 (FND-008). Both rest on at least two document evidence items. The CVC retention decision is framed as an unresolved assumption pending QSA confirmation. Refinements that keep decisions in place: the idempotency key schema (FND-001) and network tokens from launch (FND-011).

recommendation.issue: The fast-path cache key leaves out merchant identity and the request hash.
recommendation.rationale: P3 and FR-5 scope deduplication to (merchant, key) and require a 422 on body mismatch. The fast path as written breaks both before the durable path is ever reached.
recommendation.verification: Extended FR-5 replay test: cross-merchant same-key test and fast-path body-mismatch test both pass.

findings.statement: Section 9.2 caches final responses under idem:resp:{idempotency_key} and, on a hit, returns the stored response without going to DynamoDB. The key does not include merchant_id or the request hash, which contradicts P3 and FR-5. Section 9.1 says merchants often use their own order or invoice IDs, so two merchants sending the same key (for example "1001") is likely. When that happens the second merchant gets the first merchant's payment object and no payment is created for it, which can mean data disclosure and goods shipped without payment. A reused key with a different body also gets the cached response instead of HTTP 422.
findings.title: Redis idempotency fast path keyed without merchant or body hash

With asynchronous replication, writes acknowledged in the primary but not yet replicated are lost on regional loss, so RPO is bounded by replication lag, not zero. Neither Section 20 nor Section 12.3 gives the Vault or CloudHSM a recovery path in ap-southeast-3, so card payments cannot resume within the RTO.

next_step.owner: Head of Platform Engineering with Finance risk owner

recommendation.change_summary: Option 1: restate NFR-4 as RPO of at most N seconds for regional loss (zero within a region), with a reconciliation procedure for payments that were lost. Option 2: keep RPO = 0 and add a synchronous cross-region commit path for authorizations and postings, budgeting its latency in Section 21. Either way, add CDE DR (Vault data replication, a CloudHSM cluster in ap-southeast-3) to Section 20, and say how the 30-minute failover fits the NFR-3 budget.
recommendation.expected_benefit: A DR objective that can be achieved and verified, and that covers the CDE.
recommendation.issue: NFR-4 and the approved DR decision cannot both hold.
recommendation.rationale: The DR decision (Aurora Global, runbook failover) and NFR-4 contradict each other according to the document's own text, so either the requirement or the architecture has to change.
recommendation.verification: A Section 26 NFR-4 game day under write load measures actual data loss and an end-to-end card authorization in ap-southeast-3 within 30 minutes.

findings.statement: NFR-4 requires zero RPO for authorized payments and ledger postings on loss of a whole region, but Section 20.2 describes Aurora Global replication as asynchronous with typical lag under one second. Postings committed in that window can be lost. The NFR-4 game day ('unplanned failover... every ledger posting committed... is present') would therefore fail, or pass only by luck. Two things also threaten the 30-minute RTO. MSK, DynamoDB and Redis are recreated empty, which removes idempotency state. The CDE (Vault, CloudHSM) has no cross-region DR at all. Separately, one 30-minute failover is larger than the monthly downtime allowed by the 99.95% target in NFR-3.
findings.title: Zero regional RPO is impossible with asynchronous Aurora Global replication

findings.statement: Section 12.3 (and the Section 24 decision 'one HSM at launch') puts all KEKs on one HSM in ap-southeast-1a. Losing that one AZ or HSM therefore stops every card authorization, about 55% of attempts, until an HSM is restored from backup. The cascade does not help, because every acquirer path goes through the same Vault. The trigger for a second HSM (card volume above 1,500 TPS) is never reached under the 2027 target of about 1,100 card TPS. This challenges the 'one HSM at launch' decision against NFR-3 and against the three-AZ design used everywhere else (Section 20.1).

findings.statement: Section 9.3 concludes that 1,800 WCU for M-0001 is comfortable because 'a single partition sustains up to 10,000 write capacity units per second'. That figure does not match the reviewer's understanding of DynamoDB's published per-partition write limit, which must be checked. Two further assumptions are unverified. The 1,800 WCU estimate treats each write as one WCU, although response_body can be up to 4 KB. The LSI may cap the size of each partition key's item collection, which matters for a merchant writing millions of records a day. If any of these fail, the merchant with 45% of peak traffic is throttled during campaigns, which defeats NFR-1, yet Section 27 rates the Idempotency Layer 'Ready'.
findings.title: DynamoDB idempotency capacity for the largest merchant rests on an unverified limit

Items confirmed as in scope but not yet fully designed:

findings.no_change_rationale: Explicit IDs, principles, decisions and backlog give a sound basis for reviewing and verifying the design. The contradictions are handled in their own findings.
findings.statement: Every requirement has an ID and is traced to an acceptance criterion in Section 26 and a readiness verdict in Section 27. Ten numbered principles are given precedence, and confirmed decisions and the pending backlog are kept separate. That makes the design reviewable against its own intent. The weakness is that the 'principle wins' rule turns contradictions such as FND-001 and FND-002 into build ambiguity, so those sections still have to be fixed.
findings.title: Design intent is explicit and traceable

doc_anchors.quote: Journals are written in the same PostgreSQL transaction as the payment state transition that causes them,

sound_areas.why_sound: The atomic state, ledger and outbox commit and the append-only, database-enforced journals meet FR-2, FR-10, P1 and P5.

doc_anchors.quote: No floating-point type is used for amounts in any service, schema, or API payload.

sound_areas.why_sound: Signed 64-bit integer minor units, a versioned ISO 4217 exponent table, explicit adapter conversion that rejects any amount needing rounding, and a single half-to-even rounding of fees all satisfy P4 and protect the integrity of FR-10.

doc_anchors.quote: Each endpoint has a cap of 20 in-flight deliveries and its own circuit breaker, so a failing endpoint

sound_areas.why_sound: Timestamped HMAC signatures, per-endpoint secrets with rollover, a bounded at-least-once retry schedule (whose attempt count matches), a DLQ with replay, per-endpoint isolation and SSRF-safe resolution all meet FR-12 and P7 without cross-merchant starvation.

doc_anchors.quote: E-wallet and bank-transfer payments are never cascaded: the customer has already been directed to a specific wallet or

sound_areas.why_sound: Not cascading redirect and QR methods is correct, because the customer has already committed to a specific wallet or bank. This keeps FR-7 limited to cards and avoids duplicate customer-side payments.

doc_anchors.quote: write actions (manual refunds, payout holds, merchant suspension) require just-in-time elevation

sound_areas.why_sound: For staff write actions, the back-office console uses corporate SSO with hardware MFA, read-only masked defaults and just-in-time elevation approved by a second person, which meets P9 and FR-16.
